book:81884.description: The genesis of the universe elegantly explained in a simple theory based on just six numbers by one of the world's most renowned astrophysicists
commentaries: Steven Pinker references Martin Rees's book to discuss the fundamental constants that specify our universe and the concept of fine-tuning.

book:289751.description:
The act of reading is a miracle. Every new reader's brain possesses the extraordinary capacity to rearrange itself beyond its original abilities in order to understand written symbols. But how does the brain learn to read? As world-renowned cognitive neuroscientist and scholar of reading Maryanne Wolf explains in this impassioned book, we taught our brain to read only a few thousand years ago, and in the process changed the intellectual evolution of our species.
Wolf tells us that the brain that examined ti...
commentaries: Steven Pinker references this book in a list, suggesting it as a source on the science of reading.

book:1639057.description: This user-friendly, comprehensive course in probability and statistics as applied to physical and social science explains the probability calculus, distributions and densities, and the rivals of Bayesianism - the classical, logical, and subjective theories. Howson and Urbach clearly lay out the theory of classical inference, the Neyman-Pearson theory of significance tests, the classical theory of estimation, and regression analysis. The work is controversial, but gives a fair and accurate account of the ant...
commentaries: The excerpt lists this as a book reference with full bibliographic details.

book:7965510.description: For all the thousands of books that have been written about religion, few until this one have attempted to examine it scientifically: to ask why--and how--it has shaped so many lives so strongly. Is religion a product of blind evolutionary instinct or rational choice? Is it truly the best way to live a moral life? Ranging through biology, history, and psychology, Daniel C. Dennett charts religion's evolution from "wild" folk belief to "domesticated" dogma. Not an antireligious screed but an unblinking look....
commentaries: Steven Pinker lists Daniel Dennett's book 'Breaking the Spell' as part of a series of books by new atheists.

book:1853781.description:
The laws of thermodynamics drive everything that happens in the universe. From the sudden expansion of a cloud of gas to the cooling of hot metal, and from the unfurling of a leaf to the course of life itself--everything is moved or restrained by four simple laws. They establish fundamental concepts such as temperature and heat, and reveal the arrow of time and even the nature of energy itself.
Written by Peter Atkins, one of the worlds leading authorities on thermodynamics, this powerful and compact introd...
commentaries: Steven Pinker mentions Peter Atkins's book title as an example of the significance of the Second Law of Thermodynamics.
Steven Pinker lists this book in a bibliography or reference list.

book:6429163.description: The Origin of the Family, Private Property, and the State: in the light of the researches of Lewis H. Morgan is a historical materialist treatise written by Friedrich Engels and published in 1884. It is partially based on notes by Karl Marx to Lewis H. Morgan's book Ancient Society.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists these works as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_2da5932c.description: Speech delivered by Friedrich Engels at the graveside of Karl Marx on March 17, 1883, at Highgate Cemetery in London. It was first published in German in the newspaper 'Der Sozialdemokrat' on March 22, 1883.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists these works as part of a bibliography or reference list.
Hannah Arendt cites Engels alongside Marx for their neglect of the national question, which spared the socialist movement a crisis.
Hannah Arendt notes Engels's compliment to Marx, highlighting the perceived affinity between Marx's and Darwin's theories of development.

book:7805.description:
The urbane authority that Vladimir Nabokov brought to every word he ever wrote, and the ironic amusement he cultivated in response to being uprooted and politically exiled twice in his life, never found fuller expression than in Pale Firepublished in 1962 after the critical and popular success of Lolita had made him an international literary figure.
An ingeniously constructed parody of detective fiction and learned commentary, Pale Fireoffers a cornucopia of deceptive pleasures, at the center of which is a....
commentaries: Steven Pinker cites this book as an example of a great work of literature that is now cheaply and easily accessible.

book:web_2f1bb00c.description: A novel by Vladimir Nabokov originally published in Russian in 1938 as 'Priglashenie na kazn'. It tells the story of Cincinnatus C., a man sentenced to death in a surreal totalitarian state for the crime of 'gnostical turpitude'.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Nabokov's novel to present a fictional artifact that parodies both the work of time and the work of photography, showing how photographs can depersonalize and mock-possess the future.

Susan Sontag references Nabokov's novel as a literary portrait of a model totalitarian state where photography is the omnipresent art, linking it to a future dictatorship centered on 'the interesting.'

book:647942.description: In 1972, three scientists from MIT created a computer model that analyzed global resource consumption and production. Their results shocked the world and created stirring conversation about global 'overshoot, ' or resource use beyond the carrying capacity of the planet. Now, preeminent environmental scientists Donnella Meadows, Jorgen Randers, and Dennis Meadows have teamed up again to update and expand their original findings in "The Limits to Growth: The 30 Year Global Update,"Meadows, Randers, and Meadow...
commentaries: Steven Pinker cites this book as a source of failed projections about resource exhaustion.

book:18730697.description: From healthcare to workplace and campus conduct, the federal government is taking on ever more responsibility for managing our lives. At the same time, Americans have never been more disaffected with Washington, seeing it as an intrusive, incompetent, wasteful giant. Ineffective policies are caused by deep structural factors regardless of which party is in charge, bringing our government into ever-worsening disrepute. Understanding why government fails so often--and how it might become more effective--is a....
commentaries: The excerpt lists this as a book publication with publisher details.

book:web_b371c3d4.description: A philosophical work by Paul Rée analyzing the psychological and historical origins of moral concepts, influential on Nietzsche's thinking.
commentaries: Friedrich Nietzsche references Rée's book as part of a self-referential analysis, using it to illustrate the ideas of the 'first Immoralist' (himself) and the theory that there is no intelligible metaphysical world.

Friedrich Nietzsche identifies this book as the direct impulse for publishing his own hypotheses on morality, describing it as a clear, well-written, and precocious work that presented a perverse moral philosophy antithetical to his own ideas, which attracted him magnetically.

book:323203.description: In his Bellum Catilinae, C. Sallustius Crispus or Sallust (86-35/34 B.C.) recounts the dramatic events of 63 B.C., when a disgruntled and impoverished nobleman, L. Sergius Catilina, turned to armed revolution after two electoral defeats. Among his followers were a group of heavily indebted young aristocrats, the Roman poor, and a military force in the north of Italy. With his trademark archaizing style, Sallust skillfully captures the drama of the times, including an early morning attempt to assassinate the...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Sallust to support the argument that reputation and glory are governed more by chance (fortune) than by true merit.

book:web_96a9eab9.description: A controversial work by theologian David Friedrich Strauss that contrasts traditional Christian faith with modern scientific worldview, often criticized by Nietzsche as representing bourgeois complacency.
commentaries: Friedrich Nietzsche mocks David Strauss's book as a 'suburban gospel,' using it to typify German Philistine culture and smug self-content in a critical attack.

book:8104223.description: Manfred, a Faustian noble, is tortured by guilt over the death of his beloved, Astarte. He uses his mastery of language and spell-casting to summon seven spirits, from whom he seeks forgetfulness. The spirits are unable to control the past and thus cannot grant Manfred's plea.
commentaries: Friedrich Nietzsche expresses a deep personal connection to Byron's 'Manfred', finding reflections of his own soul in its dark themes from a young age.

book:web_bf8e077d.description: A philosophical work by Eugen Dühring on the value of life, referenced by Nietzsche in his critique of Dühring's philosophical system.
commentaries: Friedrich Nietzsche cites Dühring's works as examples of a scientific tendency to rehabilitate reactive emotions like revenge under the guise of justice, and he critiques Dühring's proposition about the origin of justice.

book:web_9386c3c4.description: Dühring's major philosophical work presenting his system of philosophy, which Friedrich Nietzsche critiques in 'On the Genealogy of Morals'. The work is commonly referred to as 'Course of Philosophy' in English translations.
commentaries: Friedrich Nietzsche references this book alongside 'Value of Life' to illustrate Dühring's philosophical arguments, which he opposes regarding the basis of justice in reactive feelings.

book:3535597.description:
Did God create man? Or did man create God? Famed German philosopher Ludwig Feuerbach explores the answer in this, his most influential work, published in German in 1841 and translated by celebrated English novelist George Eliot. Using Biblical references, dialectics, and ideas from some of the world's greatest thinkers, he confronts believers with his cogent explanation.
Approaching religion from a humanistic perspective, Feuerbach explores the idea that divinity is an outward projection of our idealistic h...
commentaries: Susan Sontag quotes Feuerbach's preface to illustrate a 19th-century critique of societal preference for images over reality, linking it to the advent of photography.

book:6012840.description: Don Quixotehas become so entranced by reading chivalric romances, that he determines to become a knight-errant himself. In the company of his faithful squire, Sancho Panza, his exploits blossom in all sorts of wonderful ways. While Quixote's fancy often leads him astray - he tilts at windmills, imagining them to be giants - Sancho acquires cunning and a certain sagacity. Sane madman and wise fool, they roam the world together, and together they have haunted readers' imaginations for nearly four hundred year...
commentaries: Friedrich Nietzsche contrasts the modern reader's pained reaction to the cruelty in 'Don Quixote' with the original audience's perception of it as a purely humorous work.
Jorge Luis Borges cites 'Don Quixote' as an example of a work with a sequential variety that lacks a rigid plot.
Jorge Luis Borges notes that Cervantes uses a version of the paradoxical syllogism in Don Quixote.
Jorge Luis Borges references Borges's character Pierre Menard, whose project involves Cervantes' Quixote, as an example of an extravagant literary scrutiny.
Susan Sontag analyzes the novel as a foundational epic about the addiction to reading and its consequences.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Cervantes' book 'Galatea' as a work fictionally examined within Don Quixote's library.

book:4070.description: Psychiatrist Viktor Frankl's memoir has riveted generations of readers with its descriptions of life in Nazi death camps and its lessons for spiritual survival. Between 1942 and 1945 Frankl labored in four different camps, including Auschwitz, while his parents, brother, and pregnant wife perished. Based on his own experience and the experiences of others he treated later in his practice, Frankl argues that we cannot avoid suffering but we can choose how to cope with it, find meaning in it, and move forward...
commentaries: Viktor E. Frankl directly quotes and discusses a key idea from Frankl's book 'Man’s Search for Meaning'.
Viktor E. Frankl recounts an anecdote where a soldier's psychological healing is attributed to his reading of Frankl's book.

book:web_58b4a69b.description: A foundational work of logotherapy by Viktor Frankl, originally written before his deportation to concentration camps and reconstructed in 1946. The book explores the application of logotherapy to medical practice, particularly psychiatry.
commentaries: Viktor E. Frankl references his own first book, providing its publication details.
Viktor E. Frankl notes the post-war reconstruction of Frankl's earlier book 'The Doctor and the Soul' and the rapid writing of 'Man’s Search for Meaning'.

book:2469962.description: In these selected essays, Viktor E. Franklone of the most influential thinkers of our timeillustrates the vital importance of the human dimension in psychotherapy, brilliantly celebrating each individual's unique potential.
commentaries: Viktor E. Frankl cites this work by Frankl, likely to compare or support a point, referencing specific pages.

book:88077.description: In this dizzyingly rich novel of ideas, Mann uses a sanatorium in the Swiss Alps, a community devoted exclusively to sickness, as a microcosm for Europe, which in the years before 1914 was already exhibiting the first symptoms of its own terminal irrationality. The Magic Mountain is a monumental work of erudition and irony, sexual tension and intellectual ferment, a book that pulses with life in the midst of death.
commentaries: Viktor E. Frankl references the novel to draw a parallel between the psychological state of tuberculosis patients in a sanatorium and that of prisoners in a concentration camp, both experiencing a provisional existence without a clear future or goal.
Susan Sontag cites Mann's novel to contrast the clinical and erotic meanings a photographic image (an X-ray) can hold for different characters.
Susan Sontag mentions this novel as an example of a work that employs essayistic digressions to pursue completeness.
Susan Sontag references a new translation of this novel to illustrate a trend in translation practices, specifically the handling of foreign language passages for an assumed monolingual readership.

book:21032.description: The noted Stanford University psychiatrist distills the essence of a wide range of therapies into a masterful, creative synthesis, opening up a new way of understanding each person's confrontation with four ultimate concerns: isolation, meaninglessness, death, and freedom.
commentaries: Viktor E. Frankl references Yalom's book to provide statistical evidence that meaninglessness is a significant issue in clinical populations.

book:web_c09b5648.description: A psychological study of religious sentiment and its role in personality development.
commentaries: Viktor E. Frankl cites Allport's book to support the idea that self-detachment through humor can aid in managing neurosis, directly quoting a passage that aligns with the logotherapeutic technique of paradoxical intention.

book:web_33f6d0ab.description: Foundational work in crowd psychology, analyzing how individuals behave differently in crowds. The English title is 'The Crowd: A Study of the Popular Mind'.
commentaries: Viktor E. Frankl references LeBon's book title as a known concept, using it to frame the psychological impact of the war and concentration camps.
Hannah Arendt cites Lebon's book for its mention of the selflessness characteristic of masses.

book:web_bb5d1d15.description: A cycle of ten elegies by Rainer Maria Rilke, considered his masterwork and a pinnacle of German-language poetry. They are profound meditations on human existence, love, death, and the relationship between the visible and invisible worlds.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Rilke's work to contrast the value of old, human-touched objects with modern disposability.

book:29757910.description:
'There are quantities of human beings, but there are many more faces, for each person has several.'
This dreamlike meditation on being young and alone in Paris is a feverish work of nerves, angst and sublime beauty from one of the twentieth century's greatest poets.
A new series of twenty distinctive, unforgettable Penguin Classics in a beautiful new design and pocket-sized format, with coloured jackets echoing Penguin's original covers.
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites this book as one of several that Elizabeth Hardwick found emboldening when writing 'Sleepless Nights'.

book:1343474.description: First published in 1973, this is a study of the force of photographic images which are continually inserted between experience and reality. Sontag develops further the concept of 'transparency'. When anything can be photographed and photography has destroyed the boundaries and definitions of art, a viewer can approach a photograph freely with no expectations of discovering what it means. This collection of six lucid and invigorating essays, the most famous being "In Plato's Cave", make up a deep exploration...

book:1696825.description:
Susan Sontag has said that her earliest idea of what a writer should be was "someone who is interested in everything." Thirty-five years after her first collection of essays, the now classic Against Interpretation, our most important essayist has chosen more than forty longer and shorter pieces from the last two decades that illustrate a deeply felt, kaleidoscopic array of interests, passions, observations, and ideas.
"Reading" offers ardent, freewheeling considerations of talismanic writers from her own pr...

commentaries: Susan Sontag quotes a passage from this book to illustrate a historical moment of documentation and violence.

Arhipelagul Gulag este cartea care a deschis ochii Occidentului asupra ororilor totalitarismului sovietic, aducand la lumina experientele subumane din lagarele de reeducare prin munca din URSS.
Devenita foarte repede o adevarata Biblie a disidentilor din fostul bloc sovietic, Arhipelagul Gulag este o "incercare de investigatie literara" a anilor pe care Alexandr Soljenitin (1918-2008) i-a petrecut in lagarele groazei, dupa ce criticase politica lui Stalin pe cand era capitan in armata sovietica.

commentaries: Susan Sontag references Solzhenitsyn's book as a counter-example to the Vietnam War, noting the absence of photographic evidence for the events it describes, to argue about the relationship between photography and the perception of reality.

book:597493.description: Nathaniel Hawthorne's gripping psychological drama concerns the Pyncheon family, a dynasty founded on pious theft, who live for generations under a dead man's curse until their house is finally exorcised by love.

book:47059.description:
The fragility-and the durability-of human life and art dominate this story of American expatriates in Italy in the mid-nineteenth century. Befriended by Donatello, a young Italian with the classical grace of the "Marble Faun," Miriam, Hilda, and Kenyon find their pursuit of art taking a sinister turn as Miriam's unhappy past precipitates the present into tragedy.

book:6474485.description: Nathaniel Hawthorne's most famous novel was published in 1850 and takes place in Puritan New England, focusing on a community where a beautiful young woman, Hester Prynne, and her illegitimate child are subject to persecution and ostracism; while the mother refuses to name her co-conspirator in adultery, and the father of her child burns up with secret guilt and shame. commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges critiques Hawthorne's novel The Scarlet Letter, comparing it unfavorably to his short story "Wakefield" and noting its prose quality but lack of emotional impact.

book:50776.description: Large Format for easy reading. Classic novel set in 19th-century New England, and drawing on the author's own earlier experiences at the Utopian community Brook Farm.

book:web_0664caab.description: A critical account of life in China under Mao Zedong, written by the sinologist Pierre Ryckmans under his pen name Simon Leys. It was first published in French as 'Ombres chinoises' in 1974, with the English translation appearing in 1977.

book:web_a11a3bed.description: First commercially published book illustrated with photographs, issued in six parts between 1844 and 1846. It demonstrated the potential of the calotype process and contained 24 original photographic prints.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Talbot's book to describe the origin of the photographic idea and its conceptualization as an impersonal, natural form of notation, distinct from artistic intervention.

book:60725.description: The book Let Us Now Praise Famous Men grew out of an assignment the two men accepted in 1936 to produce a magazine article on the conditions among white sharecropper families in the U.S. South during the "Dust Bowl". book:web_91e99a2d.description: A foundational work of comparative literature analyzing how reality is represented in Western writing from Homer to Virginia Woolf.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Auerbach's book to support an analysis of Balzac's literary realism.

book:1024458.description: " Un brave homme - pension bourgeoise, 600 francs de rente - s'etant depouille pour ses filles qui toutes deux ont 50 000 livres de rente, mourant comme un chien. " Telle est l'indication qu'on peut lire dans l'album de Balzac qui contient le germe du Pere Goriot. Mais ce roman est bien autre chose que le recit d'une agonie. C'est l'education sentimentale " de Rastignac, jeune provincial monte a Paris, son apprentissage de la vie, de la societe et des hommes. C'est aussi le portrait d'une ville livree au pl...
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites a specific passage from Balzac's novel as analyzed by Auerbach to illustrate a point about descriptive realism.

book:576781.description: Handsome would-be poet Lucien Chardon is poor and naive, but highly ambitious. Failing to make his name in his dull provincial hometown, he is taken up by a patroness, the captivating married woman Madame de Bargeton, and prepares to forge his way in the glamorous beau monde of Paris. But Lucien has entered a world far more dangerous than he realized, as Madame de Bargeton's reputation becomes compromised and the fickle, venomous denizens of the courts and salons conspire to keep him out of their ranks. Luc...
commentaries: Susan Sontag references these books as examples of novels with essayistic digressions that pursue completeness.

book:25934.description: Finance, fashionable society, and the intrigues of the underworld and the police system form the heart of this powerful novel, which introduces the satanic genius Vautrin, one of the greatest villains in world literature.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references these books as examples of novels with essayistic digressions that pursue completeness.

book:1154047.description: They lowered their voices and walked away in order to talk more at their ease on some retired couch. Never was a more promising mine laid open to seekers after mysteries. No one knew from what country the Lanty family came, nor to what source--commerce, extortion, piracy, or inheritance--they owed a fortune estimated at several millions. All the members of the family spoke Italian, French, Spanish, English, and German.

book:web_a33634c7.description: A foundational Bauhaus book on design and material theory, later translated as 'The New Vision: From Material to Architecture'.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Moholy-Nagy's book as a source that urged painters to learn from photographic techniques like microphotographs and aerial views.

book:web_cc9b5ce2.description: A foundational Bauhaus text exploring the relationships between visual media, where Moholy-Nagy argues for photography's capacity to create new ways of seeing distinct from traditional painting.
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites Moholy-Nagy's book to illustrate the Bauhaus view of photography as an impersonal, hygienic medium that can cleanse vision of painterly influences.

book:web_0603820e.description: A four-volume photographic work by Scottish photographer John Thomson, documenting China and its people in the late 19th century. Published between 1873-1874.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Thomson's multi-volume work as an example of photographic class tourism, documenting exotic reality abroad before turning to domestic subjects.

book:web_90dd9160.description: A landmark photobook by Albert Renger-Patzsch, featuring 100 photographs that exemplify the 'New Objectivity' (Neue Sachlichkeit) movement. The title translates to 'The World Is Beautiful' and the work is known for its precise, detailed images of natural and industrial subjects.
commentaries: Susan Sontag cites Renger-Patzsch's book as an early photographic best-seller that presented close-up images to showcase the world's beauty.

book:10066225.description: The Day of the Locustis a novel about Hollywood and its corrupting touch, about the American dream turned into a sun-drenched California nightmare. Nathaniel West's Hollywood is not the glamorous "home of the stars" but a seedy world of little people, some hopeful, some desparing, all twisted by their by their own desires -- from the ironically romantic artist narrator to a macho movie cowboy, a middle-aged innocent from America's heartland, and the hard-as-nails call girl would-be-star whom they all lust a...
commentaries: Susan Sontag references West's novel as an example of 1930s literature that treated certain subjects with anguish, contrasting it with 1960s artistic treatments.

book:250041.description: As described by Atkinson in the NY Times: "A scornful feature editor of a newspaper picks an ambitious young reporter to conduct the advice of the lovelorn column. As time goes on, the genuineness of the agony in the letters that come in gets under the skin of the columnist. He is distressed to find himself presiding over a monst...

book:6048685.description: Cartier-Bresson's concept of the "decisive moment" -- a split second that reveals the larger truth of a situation -- shaped modern street photography and set the stage for hundreds of photojournalists to bring the world into living rooms through magazines.
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Cartier-Bresson's book to illustrate his initial technical justification for preferring black-and-white photography, later noting that Cartier-Bresson shifted to a principled stance against color as technology improved.

book:864395.description: In this hallucinatory novel, the car provides the hellish tableau in which Vaughan, a "TV scientist" turned "nightmare angel of the highways," experiments with erotic atrocities among auto crash victims, each more sinister than the last. James Ballard, his friend and fellow obsessive, tells the story of this twisted visionary as he careens rapidly toward his own demise in an intentionally orchestrated car crash with Elizabeth Taylor. A classic work of cutting edge fiction, Crash explores the disturbing pote...
commentaries: Susan Sontag references Ballard's novel as an example of using collected photographs to feed and eroticize a specific, obsessive fantasy.

book:679940.description: Roaming Paris streets by night in the early 1930s, Brassa created arresting images of the city's dramatic nocturnal landscape. First published in French in 1932, this new edition brings one of Brassa's finest works back into print. The back alleys, metro stations, and bistros he photographed are at turns hauntingly empty or peopled by prostitutes, laborers, thugs, and lovers. commentaries: Susan Sontag references Brassai's book as an example of the flaneur's findings, illustrating the depiction of urban dramas of sex and loneliness.

book:364194.description: For Naked City, his first collection, Weegee cruised the streets of 1940s New York in the wee hours in search of the sensational. Lewd, louche, licentious but always brimming with life (except when brimming with death), Weegee's photographs have endured decades of modern art criticism and are again enjoying a much-deserved cult revival.
commentaries: Susan Sontag mentions Weegee's book as an example of the flaneur's perspective, portraying the city as a theater of disaster.

commentaries: Susan Sontag references Anderson's book to illustrate a literary treatment of small-town misery and the concept of the grotesque, linking it to the Surrealist perspective in photography.

book:web_8540c1ae.description: Collected works of Bertolt Brecht published in exile by Malik Verlag in London, 1938.

book:882203.description:

The title translates to 'Attic Nights', referring to long winter nights spent in Attica.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Aulus Gellius's 'Attic Nights' to argue that excessive reliance on subordinates' judgment undermines authority.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Aulus Gellius's work as containing a version of a paradoxical syllogism, similar to others mentioned.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Aulus Gellius's 'Attic Nights' as a source for the story of Archytas's flying dove, connecting it to Wilkins's predictions about lunar travel.

book:3227621.description: "Sources and Backgrounds" includes Seneca's inspired commentary on Ovid, Charles Martin's essay on the ways in which pantomimic dancing--an art form popular in Ovid's time--may have been the model forMetamorphoses, as well as related works by Virgil, Callimachus, Hesiod, and Lucretius, among others. From the enormous body of scholarly writing onMetamorphoses, Charles Martin has chosen six major interpretations by Bernard Knox, J. R. R. Mackail, Norman O. Brown, Italo Calvino, Frederick Ahl, and Diane Middle...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's 'Metamorphoses' to use the myth of Niobe as an allegory for the stupefying effect of overwhelming grief, linking it to the theme of sorrow's physical manifestations.
Michel de Montaigne recalls that his earliest enjoyment of books came from reading Ovid's Metamorphoses in childhood, finding it the easiest and most age-appropriate text available to him.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's Metamorphoses to convey a willingness to entrust future events to fortune.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid to describe a scene of extreme cold where wine froze solid and was distributed in pieces.
Michel de Montaigne cites Ovid's 'Tristia' to illustrate the paradoxical pleasure found in weeping.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's Tristia to describe his own natural inclination towards avoiding troubles and seeking a quiet life.

book:20385662.description: The Ars amatoria (English: The Art of Love) is an instructional book series elegy in three books by Ancient Rome Roman poet Ovid. It was written in 2 AD. It is about teaching basic Gentlemanly male and female relationship skills and techniques. Ovid offers advice to men on subjects such as, how to seduce and keep a woman, and also notably offers women advice on how to be attractive to men. He advises that, "if one is accompanying a lady to the horse-racing in the Circus Maximus, one should gallantly brush t...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's Ars Amatoria to vividly describe the physical distortions of anger, illustrating why it impairs judgment.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's 'Ars Amatoria' (The Art of Love) to argue against jealousy, suggesting love is not diminished by being shared.

book:20738843.description:
This is an alternate cover edition for ISBN13: 9780140423556
In the twenty-one poems of the "Heroides", Ovid gave voice to the heroines and heroes of epic and myth. These deeply moving literary epistles reveal the happiness and torment of love, as the writers tell of their pain at separation, forgiveness of infidelity or anger at betrayal. The faithful Penelope wonders at the suspiciously long absence of Ulysses, while Dido bitterly reproaches Aeneas for too eagerly leaving her bed to follow his destiny, an...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid to express personal experience where cunning or worldly wisdom failed, while straightforwardness succeeded.

book:3077838.description: Ovid's "Amores" translated by Guy Lee in the 1960s.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references Ovid's 'Amores' to humorously underscore the extent and endurance of his youthful sexual vigor.
Michel de Montaigne cites Ovid's work to support the idea that imagination can transmit harm, similar to physical contagion.

book:web_82842cb9.description: A scholarly treatise on Roman assemblies and political institutions by the French humanist Nicolas de Grouchy (c. 1510–1572). The work analyzes the comitia (popular assemblies) of ancient Rome and was influential in Renaissance political thought.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions Nicolas Grouchy as one of his domestic tutors and notes his authorship of a book on Roman assemblies.

book:144513.description: ..". gives us all sixteen of the satires in the tough, slashing manner of the original, unheard in Dryden and the few others who tried it." --Saturday Review
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Juvenal to support the philosophical argument that glory, in and of itself, is worthless.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal's Satires to illustrate the commonness of valiant deaths and their lack of lasting renown.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal's 'Satires' to vividly describe the furious rage of parents beating their children, emphasizing the intensity of their anger.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal's Satires to argue that a citizen's value lies in their utility to the state, framing the discussion on child-rearing.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Juvenal to satirize the learned who excessively parade their knowledge in all discourse, even in intimate matters.

book:11381743.description: The date of composition of the Metamorphoses is uncertain. It's variously been considered by scholars as a youthful work preceding Apuleius' Apology of 158/9, or as the climax of his literary career & perhaps as late as the 170s or 180s. Apuleius adapted the story from a Greek original of which the author's name is said to be Lucius of Patrae (the name of the lead character & narrator). This Greek text has been lost, but there is Loukios e onos (Loukios e onos, Loukios/Lucius or the Ass), a similar tale of....
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites 'The Golden Ass' as an example of the nomadic, random genre of adventure narratives, alongside other works like 'Don Quixote'.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions 'The Golden Ass' as an example of a work with a sequential, less rigid plot structure.

book:1209722.description: The Adelphoe (The Brothers) of Terence is a Latin adaptation of a comedy of the same name by the Greek comic playwright Menander. The theme of the play is the perennially interesting question of the relationship between the generations and the proper way to bring up a son. In the introduction Mr Martin considers Terence in the context of Roman comedy generally and discusses the background of the Adelphoe. There is also a section on metre and scansion and a short analysis of the textual tradition. The full a...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Terence's Adelphoe to express despair over the irredeemable state of society.

book:1062328.description:
Terence brought to the Roman stage a bright comic voice and a refined sense of style. His six comedies - first produced in the half dozen years before his premature death in 159 B.C. - imaginatively reformulated in Latin plays written by Greek playwrights, especially Menander.
For this new Loeb Classical Library edition of Terence, John Barsby gives us a faithful and lively translation with full explanatory notes, facing a freshly edited Latin text.
Volume I contains a substantial introduction and three pla...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Terence's Heauton Timorumenos to articulate his self-imposed abstinence from pleasure in the absence of his friend, underscoring their shared existence.
Michel de Montaigne quotes a line from Terence's play 'Heauton Timorumenos' to illustrate a point about personal appearance and interpretation.

Michel de Montaigne quotes Martial's epigram to recount the story of Arria and Paetus, using it to highlight the nobility and courage of Arria's action, though he notes that the poet's expression falls short of the action's true bravery.

book:web_2fd9b58b.description: A Latin poem in elegiac couplets describing the author's sea voyage from Rome to Gaul in 416 CE. The work is often cited as 'Itinerarium' or 'De Reditu Suo' and contains the quoted line about the plague spreading when lanced.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Rutilius to present a view that punishment may spread vice rather than curb it.

book:38154.description: The only unabridged prose translation of Ariosto's Orlando Furioso- a witty parody of the chivalric legends of Charlemagne and the Saracen invasion of France - this version faithfully recaptures the entire narrative and the subtle meanings behind it.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ariosto's epic poem to illustrate the idea that true virtue lies in performing brave actions for their own sake, not for the sake of being witnessed or narrated.

book:web_4ae70c45.description: Collection of elegiac letters written by Ovid during his exile to Tomis on the Black Sea, addressed to various friends and supporters in Rome, pleading for his recall.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's verse from 'De Ponto' to express his own dissatisfaction with his writings, using it as a comparison to illustrate his self-criticism.
Michel de Montaigne quotes Ovid's 'De Ponto' to emphasize that no authority can justify betraying a friend, even for public service.
Michel de Montaigne references Ovid's 'De Pont' to illustrate the Roman custom of kissing in greeting.

book:web_5b36bd59.description: A panegyric poem by Claudian celebrating the sixth consulship of the Roman Emperor Honorius in 404 AD. It is a major work of Late Latin literature.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites a Latin verse from Claudius to support the argument that true victory lies in subduing the enemy's spirit.

book:web_cd3a8aca.description: One of the books of the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament, traditionally attributed to King Solomon. It is a philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, famously declaring 'Vanity of vanities; all is vanity.'
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references the Book of Ecclesiastes to underscore the theme of vanity, which he is meditating upon in his essay.

book:web_ed66ea85.description: A lost work by Antisthenes, founder of Cynic philosophy, referenced in ancient sources but not extant. Likely discussed themes of education, mentorship, and relationships between teacher and student.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions two books by Antisthenes, with alternative titles, questioning their subjects in a list of works on love and procreation.

book:web_e9e32c11.description: A lost work by Antisthenes, the founder of Cynic philosophy, referenced by ancient authors. The title suggests it was a philosophical treatise on marriage and procreation.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions two books by Antisthenes, with alternative titles, questioning their subjects in a list of works on love and procreation.

book:web_a73db2bc.description: A methodological work on how to study and understand history, written by the French jurist and political philosopher Jean Bodin. It presents a systematic approach to historical study and is considered an important early work in historiography.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions Jean Bodin's work 'Methodus ad facilem historiarum cognitionem' as having sufficiently addressed the obscurity of self-knowledge in historical matters.

book:web_80662323.description: A lost work on love by the Stoic philosopher Cleanthes, mentioned in ancient sources such as Diogenes Laërtius' 'Lives of the Philosophers' (3rd century CE).
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions two books by Cleanthes, questioning their content in a list of philosophical works on love.

book:web_2a3a829e.description: A philosophical dialogue on love, attributed to Demetrius of Phalerum (c. 350–280 BCE), an Athenian orator and Peripatetic philosopher. The work is known from ancient references but is now lost.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions a specific book by Demetrius Phalereus, questioning its content in a list of works on love.

book:505222.description: In the early 1500s five men and five women find themselves trapped by floods and compelled to take refuge in an abbey high in the Pyrenees. When told they must wait days for a bridge to be repaired, they are inspired - by recalling Boccaccio's Decameron - to pass the time in a cultured manner by each telling a story every day. The stories, however, soon degenerate into a verbal battle between the sexes, as the characters weave tales of corrupt friars, adulterous noblemen and deceitful wives. From the cynica...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references a specific tale in the 'Heptameron' by the Queen of Navarre, disagreeing with its portrayal of a chaste encounter as miraculous, while also offering a brief positive comment on the book itself.

book:web_bc0ebfd0.description: A collection of biographies of famous men, including a biography of Titus Pomponius Atticus. The 'Life of Atticus' is one of the surviving sections of this work.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne concludes with a quote from Cornelius Nepos to assert that individual character, rather than external power, shapes one's fortune.

book:15953862.description: Drawn from James B. Atkinson and David Sices' Montaigne: Selected Essays, this annotated translation of Etienne de La Boetie's political masterpiece offers an ideal opportunity to become acquainted with the thought of a brilliant though short-lived sixteenth-century French thinker known for "his mortal and sworn hatred for all vice," as his friend Michel de Montaigne put it, "but particularly for that sordid traffic concocted under the honorable title of justice." Atkinson's Introduction fleshes out a portr...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne borrows this discourse by Estienne de la Boetie to adorn his own work, praising it as finely written and full, though noting it was written in youth and falls short of what Boetie might have achieved later.
Michel de Montaigne suggests that a brief comment in Plutarch may have inspired La Boetie's book 'Voluntary Servitude'.

book:web_aa1e3fbc.description: A collection of pastoral poems falsely attributed to the Roman poet Gallus (Gaius Cornelius Gallus, c. 70–26 BCE) in the Renaissance. The actual author is unknown, but the poems circulated under this pseudonym in the 16th century and were included in early printed editions of Virgil's works.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne quotes a passage from Pseudo-Gallus's 'Eclogues' to illustrate the oppressive nature of life under strict regimens, using it to argue against depriving oneself of accustomed pleasures.

book:527507.description: In The Book of the Courtier (1528), Baldesar Castiglione, a diplomat and Papal Nuncio to Rome, sets out to define the essential virtues for those at Court. In a lively series of imaginary conversations between the real-life courtiers to the Duke of Urbino, his speakers discuss qualities of noble behaviour - chiefly discretion, decorum, nonchalance and gracefulness - as well as wider questions such as the duties of a good government and the true nature of love. Castiglione's narrative power and psychological...
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Castiglione's 'The Courtier' for its opinion on the social disgrace of riding a mule.

book:15777533.description:
Ideale rappresentante dell'autunno del Rinascimento, la Gerusalemme liberatadivenne ben presto uno tra i libri piu letti e amati in tutta Europa.
Tasso seppe descrivere con il suo poema un mondo umano e narrativo chiaroscurale, ricco di una tensione mai completamente risolta tra etica e desiderio, tra doveri nei confronti di una giustizia superiore e umanissimi cedimenti alle debolezze. Nel contrasto allargato alle grandi forze del Cielo e dell'Inferno, la Liberatacomunica un profondo senso di crisi attrave...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges uses Tasso's epic poem as an example of a work from which allegorical meanings can be derived.
Jorge Luis Borges discusses Tasso's 'Gerusalemme liberate' as a notable epic poem, contrasting it with its less successful revision.
Jorge Luis Borges references Tasso's epic poem as the third and least successful variation of a motif originating in Homer.

book:web_e6634e53.description: A revised version of Tasso's epic poem 'Gerusalemme Liberata' (Jerusalem Delivered), written to conform more strictly to Counter-Reformation religious orthodoxy and Aristotelian literary principles. It is generally considered artistically inferior to the original.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Tasso's 'Conquistata' as a revised version of his epic that failed to achieve literary significance.
Jorge Luis Borges mentions Tasso alongside Milton and Virgil as poets committed to their craft.

book:9076267.description:
Testo latino a fronte.
A military leader of legendary genius, Caesar was also a great writer, recording the events of his life with incomparable immediacy and power The Civil Waris a tense and gripping depiction of his struggle with Pompey over the leadership of Republican Rome - a conflict that spanned the entire Roman world, from Gaul and Spain to Asia and Africa. Where Caesar's own account leaves off in 48 BC, his lieutenants take up the history, describing the vital battles of Munda, Spain and Thapsus,....
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites Caesar's 'De Bello Civili' to illustrate that the Roman practice of fighting with rapier and cloak was similar to a contemporary custom.

book:web_ce36d4e5.description: A collection of neo-Latin love poems (kisses) by the Dutch poet Johannes Secundus, first published posthumously in 1539. The work was highly influential in Renaissance poetry and inspired many imitations.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne cites the Basia as a pleasant modern work, though he questions if it fits the title of 'book'.

book:web_f120e8a2.description: A collection of moralizing letters by Spanish bishop and chronicler Antonio de Guevara, commonly known in English as 'Golden Epistles' or 'Familiar Epistles'. The work was widely popular across Europe in the 16th century.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne mentions obtaining information from Guevara's 'Letters' (referred to as 'Golden Epistles') but expresses a low personal opinion of the work.

book:web_02f930ae.description: A collection of historical anecdotes and sayings in nine books, compiled during the reign of Tiberius (14–37 AD). Commonly known as 'Memorable Deeds and Sayings' or simply 'Valerius Maximus'.
commentaries: Michel de Montaigne references Valerius Maximus as a source for an anecdote about a death caused by a grape-stone, exemplifying death's trivial causes.
Michel de Montaigne cites Valerius Maximus for an extreme example of thirst during a siege in Crete.
Michel de Montaigne references Valerius Maximus's 'Factorum ac Dictorum Memorabilium Libri IX' to argue that compelled actions credit the enforcer rather than the performer.
Michel de Montaigne references Valerius Maximus to critique the decline of military discipline.

book:web_b6c71cf3.description: A historical study of Russian foreign policy and influence in the Balkan region, published by Oxford University Press.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists two books by B. H. Sumner as part of a bibliography or reference list.
Hannah Arendt cites this book to reference Dulles's explanation of the CIA's role.
Hannah Arendt cites Allan W. Dulles's statement to support the claim about the influential position of intelligence services in the U.S. government.

book:web_35c0f407.description: A legal and administrative work by Hans Frank, a prominent Nazi jurist and Governor-General of occupied Poland, published in Munich in 1939.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Frank's book to illustrate the ideological presentation of the Nazi regime as based on loyalty rather than dictatorship.

book:web_86a28b6d.description: A historical study of the Pan-German League (Alldeutscher Verband), a German nationalist organization active from 1890 to 1918, published as part of the 'Historische Studien' monograph series.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Werner's book as a source of useful information on the Pan-German League.

book:web_fd2f37d9.description: A history of Bolshevism from its origins to the early 1930s, written by the German Marxist historian Arthur Rosenberg. Originally published in German in 1932 as 'Geschichte des Bolschewismus'.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Rosenberg's book for a detailed description of how party members destroyed the Soviet system from within.
Hannah Arendt references Rosenberg's book to illustrate the dual structure of power in Soviet Russia, contrasting the formal Soviet government with the actual rule of the Bolshevik Party.

book:web_409619b9.description: A 10-volume universal cultural history of humanity by German ethnographer and librarian Gustav Friedrich Klemm, published between 1843 and 1852. It was an influential early work in the field of cultural anthropology and ethnology.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Klemm's cultural history, possibly as an early work in anthropology.

book:691614.description:
Originally published 1937; this is a reprint of the second edition of 1948.
Nikolai Berdyaev (1874-1948), born into the Russian aristocratic intelligentsia, was, as a young Marxist, sentenced in 1897 to three years of internal exile for illegal political activity.
After turning from Marxism toward Christianity, his 1913 criticism of the Orthodox Church led him to be charged with blasphemy, a crime for which he would have been liable to permanent Siberian exile, though WWI and the 1917 Revolution prevented h...
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Berdyaev's book for a specific page on Russian communism.
Hannah Arendt cites Berdyaev's book, likely to reference an analysis of Russian communism.

book:web_2f324756.description: A study of Soviet foreign policy and internal politics by the Russian-born American historian and political writer David J. Dallin, analyzing the transition from Stalinist purges to post-Stalin international relations.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists this book as part of a bibliography or reference list.
Hannah Arendt references Dallin's work on Soviet concentration camps, noting its sometimes less convincing nature due to sources from prominent personalities.
Hannah Arendt references Dallin's book to critique the economic theory of Russian camps, noting Dallin's own admission of labor inefficiency.
Hannah Arendt cites Dallin's work as a source for statistics on the shortage of prison space in Russia in 1925–26.

book:web_4cd69ad8.description: A study of the Soviet forced labor camp system (Gulag) published by two Russian-born scholars and anti-communist writers.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites this book for statistics on forced labor and death rates in Russian labor camps.
Hannah Arendt lists this book as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_20fee2f4.description: A seminal analysis of the political, economic, and social structure of Nazi Germany, arguing that Nazism represented a form of totalitarian monopoly capitalism and a collapse of the traditional state into a chaotic 'Behemoth'.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Neumann's book as a reference for understanding the party-state relationship in totalitarian regimes.
Hannah Arendt quotes Neumann's work to illustrate a perspective on the nature of Nazi Germany.

book:web_649ff935.description: A collection of letters by T. E. Lawrence ('Lawrence of Arabia'), edited by David Garnett and published in 1939.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Lawrence's letters, edited by Garnett, to provide an instance of 'pacification' methods in the Near East as described by Lawrence.
Hannah Arendt lists this book as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_480e39dc.description: David Rousset's account of his experiences in Nazi concentration camps, originally published in French as 'L'Univers concentrationnaire' (1946). The English translation 'The Other Kingdom' was published in 1947 and was influential in documenting the concentration camp system.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Rousset's book in the context of discussing the protective wall of incredulity around Nazi atrocities.

book:web_8ef4f77c.description: A seminal work by French writer and political activist David Rousset, based on his own experience as a prisoner in Nazi concentration camps. It was one of the first detailed accounts of the camp system and won the Prix Renaudot in 1946.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt credits Rousset as the first to understand a particular aspect of the concentration camp phenomenon.
Hannah Arendt quotes Rousset's work to describe the incredulity of prisoners and outsiders regarding the horrors of concentration camps.
Hannah Arendt cites a specific page from Rousset's work for further detail.
Hannah Arendt cites Rousset's work to support the claim that life in a concentration camp was a prolonged process of dying.

book:web_fc1836b7.description: A scholarly study of Ernst Moritz Arndt's role in the German national awakening movement, published by Columbia University Press.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt cites Pundt's book as a source for information about Ernst Moritz Arndt and nationalism.
Hannah Arendt references Pundt's book as the source for a translation, though the excerpt is cut off.

book:web_572392c7.description: A book by Louis Dimier chronicling twenty years of the Action Française, a French monarchist and anti-republican movement.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Dimier's book as a source on attempts to win workers with antisemitic slogans and the actions of Léon Daudet.

book:web_5eeb3c09.description: A key ideological text of Nazi Germany, written by the party's chief ideologue Alfred Rosenberg. It promoted racist and antisemitic theories, arguing for the superiority of the 'Aryan' race and the need to combat 'Jewish influence.'
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Rosenberg's book to contrast it with scholarly work, implying it is a work of charlatanism rather than genuine scholarship.

book:1946717.description: The Myth of the Twentieth Century (German: Der Mythus des zwanzigsten Jahrhunderts) by Alfred Rosenberg, one of the principal ideologues of the Nazi party and editor of the Nazi paper Volkischer Beobachter. It was the most influential Nazi text after Hitler's Mein Kampf. The titular "myth" is "the myth of blood, which under the sign of the swastika unchains the racial world-revolution. It is the awakening of the race soul, which after long sleep victoriously ends the race...
commentaries: Hannah Arendt critiques Rosenberg's book for its ideological error in admitting racial pluralism, which violated Nazi exclusionary principles.

book:web_4eb0296f.description: A biography of Friedrich Schleiermacher, the German theologian and philosopher, written by Wilhelm Dilthey. The work is considered an important contribution to intellectual history and biography.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt references Dilthey's biography of Schleiermacher as a prime source for understanding Jewish society in late 18th-century Berlin.

book:web_7f43a051.description: A biographical work about Georges Clemenceau, the French statesman, during his retirement years, written by journalist and writer René Benjamin.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt uses Benjamin's book to quote a remark by Clemenceau expressing his loss of faith in democracy.

book:web_3a2b30d8.description: A work by German colonial administrator and politician Heinrich Schnee, examining the relationship between nationalism and imperialism in the early 20th century.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists a book by Heinrich Schnee as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:web_aa53a90d.description: A foundational Marxist analysis of capitalism, arguing that the fusion of banking and industrial capital into 'finance capital' leads to imperialism and the end of competitive capitalism.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt notes that Hilferding's book mentions, but does not fully analyze, imperialism's revival of primitive accumulation methods.
Hannah Arendt references Stalin's book as a source, citing a specific volume and chapter.
Hannah Arendt references Stalin's work 'Leninism' for his report denouncing deviations within the Party.

book:web_c36df213.description: A collection of speeches and writings by Joseph Stalin, originally published in Russian and later translated into English. The work presents Stalin's interpretation and application of Marxist-Leninist theory.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists several books by J. V. Stalin as part of a bibliography or reference list.
Hannah Arendt cites a statement by Stalin, likely from a speech or written work, to illustrate the scale of promotions following purges in the Soviet Union.

book:web_a325b00f.description: A brief and reliable account of the Dreyfus Affair and its impact on the French Third Republic, published in 1930.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt describes Charensol's work as brief and reliable.
Hannah Arendt references G. Charensol's work on the complicity of the Haute Banque in the Orleanist movement.

book:web_dbd13333.description: A collection of Stalin's writings and speeches on Leninism, published in English translation in London in 1933.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists several books by J. V. Stalin as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:1423460.description: Voltaire, avec son esprit acerbe et sa plume subtile, a trouve dans la forme du dictionnaire une voie royale d'expression qui lui permis d'echapper a la censure de son temps. Utilisant le jeu des renvois entre les definitions pour tromper la vigilance des autorites et inserant ses analyses les plus iconoclastes dans la definition de termes anodins, Voltaire se livre a un jeu de piste a l'attention d'un lecteur averti, incite a concevoir ce dictionnaire comme un veritable rebus. Ainsi, a l'article Idolatrie,...
commentaries: Hannah Arendt notes Voltaire's entry in his philosophical dictionary regarding racial differences.

book:1362044.description: Candidenous conte les mesaventures d'un voyageur philosophe qui affronte les horreurs de la guerre et les sanglants caprices de la Nature ; qui connait les desillusions de l'amour et decouvre les turpitudes de ses semblables, faisant a l'occasion l'experience de leurs dangereuses fantaisies. Pourtant si l'homme est un bien mechant animal et si l'existence n'est qu'une cascade de catastrophes, est-ce une raison pour que le heros perde sa serenite et le recit de son allegresse ? Sous la forme d'une ironique f...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Faguet's critique that Flaubert was influenced by memories of characters from Voltaire's 'Candide'.
Susan Sontag cites Voltaire's 'Candide' as a conscious literary reference influencing her own first novel, seen as a satire on optimism.

book:web_d3addb47.description: A philosophical tale by Voltaire, first published in 1768, telling the story of the Babylonian princess Formosante and her quest to find her destined husband.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Voltaire's 'La Princesse de Babylone' as a book that influenced Beckford, based on Chapman's research.

book:web_345e5b6a.description: A pamphlet by Talleyrand, written in 1799, advocating for the establishment of new colonies. It was later reprinted in the 'Annales' of the Académie des Sciences Coloniales in 1929.
commentaries: Hannah Arendt lists a work by C. M. de Talleyrand as part of a bibliography or reference list.

book:392274.description: "Youth" is an autobiographical short story by Joseph Conrad. Written in 1898, it was first published in Blackwood's Magazine, and included as the first story in the 1902 volume Youth, a Narrative, and Two Other Stories. This volume also includes Heart of Darkness and The End of the Tether, stories concerned with the themes of maturity and old age, respectively. "Youth" depicts a young man's first journey to the East. It is narrated by Charles Marlow who is also the narrator of Lord Jim and Chance. The narra...
commentaries: Hannah Arendt describes Conrad's work as the most illuminating on race experience in Africa.
Hannah Arendt cites Joseph Conrad's phrase to characterize the scramble for Africa and investment fever.
Hannah Arendt references Conrad's ideas to describe the isolated and lawless existence of the Boers, using his imagery to underscore their detachment from civilized society.

book:12984120.description: Heyst was not conscious of either friends or of enemies. It was the very essence of his life to be a solitary achievement, accomplished not by hermit-like withdrawal with its silence and immobility, but by a system of restless wandering, by the detachment of an impermanent dweller amongst changing scenes.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes Joseph Conrad's statement about the reality of a character in his novel Victory to illustrate how novelists typically believe in their characters, contrasting this with Hawthorne's method.

book:86658.description:
Mr Verloc, the secret agent, keeps a shop in London's Soho where he lives with his wife Winnie, her infirm mother, and her idiot brother, Stevie. When Verloc is reluctantly involved in an anarchist plot to blow up the Greenwich Observatory things go disastrously wrong, and what appears to be "a simple tale" proves to involve politicians, policemen, foreign diplomats and London's fashionable society in the darkest and most surprising interrelations.
Based on the text which Conrad's first English readers enjo...

book:web_2b2e41b0.description: Second volume in Anatole France's four-volume series 'Histoire contemporaine' (1896-1901), a satirical chronicle of French provincial life and politics during the Third Republic.

book:2425582.description:
This is the testament of Paul Baumer, who enlists with his classmates in the German army of World War I. These young men become enthusiastic soldiers, but their world of duty, culture, and progress breaks into pieces under the first bombardment in the trenches.

book:web_a0a5f548.description: A study of the language and jargon used by Spanish criminals in the late 19th century, written by criminologist Rafael Salillas.

book:web_8d7f2413.description: A prose work by John Donne defending the thesis that suicide is not necessarily a mortal sin. Written circa 1608 but published posthumously in 1644.

book:web_57c73833.description: Historical work by Argentine writer Leopoldo Lugones about the Jesuit missions in South America, particularly the Jesuit reductions in Paraguay and surrounding regions.

book:7029455.description: This classic work is a general introduction to Indian philosophy that covers the Vedic and Epic periods, including expositions on the hymns of the Rig Veda, the Upanisads, Jainism, Buddhism and the theism of the Bhagvadgita. commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges reviews a specific book attributed to Lord Halifax, 'Ghost Book', indicating a direct citation of the work.

Boethius composed De Consolation Philosophiaein the 6th century while awaiting death by torture, condemned on a charge of plotting against Gothic rule, which he protested as manifestly unjust. Though a Christian, Boethius details the true end of life as the soul's knowledge of God, and consoles himself with the tenets of Greek philosophy, not with Christian precepts.

Gabriel Syme is a poet and a police detective. Lucian Gregory is a poet and a bomb-throwing anarchist. book:677058.description: In the early years of the thirteenth century the Danish writer Saxo Grammaticus provided his people with a History of the Danes, an account of their glorious past from the legendary kings and heroes of Denmark to the historical present. Here Hilda Ellis Davidson, a specialist in Scandinavian m...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes from Saxo Grammaticus's 'Gesta Danorum' to support his point about Icelandic historians impartially recording history.

book:web_68b2a577.description: A pioneering encyclopedia of Islamic, Middle Eastern, and Asian history, geography, and culture, compiled by the French orientalist Barthélemy d'Herbelot. It was a major reference work for European scholars of the Orient throughout the 18th and 19th centuries.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges lists d'Herbelot's 'Bibliotheque orientale' as one of the works that influenced Beckford, according to his biographer Chapman.

book:352047.description:
J.W. Dunne (1866-1949) was an accomplished English aeronautical engineer and a designer of Britian's early military aircraft. His An Experiment with Time, first published in 1927, sparked a great deal of scientific interest in--and controversy about--his new model of multidimensional time.

commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references a specific chapter in Dunne's book 'An Experiment with Time' to outline his argument on consciousness.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Dunne's book to discuss a concept of perpendicular time, referencing a specific chapter.

book:94486.description:
Jorge Luis Borges declared The Invention of Morela masterpiece of plotting, comparable to The Turn of the Screwand Journey to the Center of the Earth. Set on a mysterious island, Bioy's novella is a story of suspense and exploration, as well as a wonderfully unlikely romance, in which every detail is at once crystal clear and deeply mysterious.
Inspired by Bioy Casares's fascination with the movie star Louise Brooks, The Invention of Morelhas gone on to live a secret life of its own. Greatly admired by Juli...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges introduces Bioy Casares' novel as the subject of discussion, highlighting its plot and significance.
Jorge Luis Borges again references Bioy Casares' novel, placing it among other works with admirable plots.

book:web_1750656e.description: An English translation and study of the Chinese Taoist philosopher Zhuangzi (Chuang Tzu) by the British diplomat and sinologist Herbert Allen Giles. This was the first complete English translation of the Zhuangzi text.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Giles's book as the source for the story of Chuang Tzu's dream.

book:19101869.description: The Finnegans Wake Notebook Edition is a fully integrated and cross-referenced edition of all the extant work-books compiled by Joyce after the completion of Ulysses. It will be published as a series of fascicles, one per authorial notebook, three per scribal notebook, fifty-five in all. This will make individual notebooks available to scholars as they appear and allow critical feedback, laying the foundations for an electronic edition that will be prepared simultaneously. The editorial aim is to bring toge...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Joyce's 'Finnegans Wake' as an even more demanding and incomprehensible work than 'Ulysses', whose readers are deemed inconceivable.
Jorge Luis Borges references Joyce's work as an example of literary experimentation with time and simultaneity.
Susan Sontag presents this book as a unique counter-example to the idea that anything can be translated, arguing its multilingual nature makes it untranslatable.

book:15956695.description: 'Ulysses', one of the greatest novels of the 20th century, has had a profound influence on modern fiction. In a series of episodes covering the course of a single day, 16 June 1904, the novel traces the movements of Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus through the streets of Dublin.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references T.S. Eliot's review of 'Ulysses' to support the idea of new literature being based on old myths.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Joyce's novel as the prime example of a work where every detail is a prophecy, illustrating a magical causal procedure.
Jorge Luis Borges references Joyce's novel 'Ulysses' as a work that demands extraordinary cognitive abilities to read, comparing its reader to the fictional character Funes.

Susan Sontag suggests that Döblin drew inspiration from Joyce's Ulysses for Berlin Alexanderplatz.

Susan Sontag mentions this book as an example of a challenging text that is often cited in arguments about translatability, implying it is a work for which the claim 'anything can be translated' is tested.

book:web_1a673591.description: A novel by English author Eden Phillpotts, published in 1934. Phillpotts (1862-1960) was a prolific writer of novels, plays, and poetry, best known for his Dartmoor-based works.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Phillpotts' work as another example of a detective novel with psychological elements.

book:web_8de3518f.description: A scholarly work on the Eleatic school of pre-Socratic philosophy, focusing on Parmenides, Zeno, and Melissus. Albertelli was an Italian philosopher and anti-fascist resistance fighter.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Albertelli's book 'Gli Eleati' as a source for interpreting Parmenides' concept of the sphere.

book:web_b335d4cb.description: An epic poem in continuation of Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso', focusing on the character Angelica. The work is often referred to simply as 'Angélica'. Canto XI is referenced in Borges's text.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Barahona de Soto's epic poem as another example of the paradoxical syllogism structure.

book:web_16174475.description: An essay or short work by Hilaire Belloc, likely included in one of his collections, where he discusses William Beckford and compares his prose to Voltaire's.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Belloc's book for its opinion on Beckford, comparing his prose to Voltaire's and condemning his character.

book:30231779.description: Considered by Rumi to be "the master" of Sufi mystic poetry, Attar is best known for his epic poem The Conference of the Birds, a magnificent allegorical tale about the soul's search for meaning. The poem recounts the perilous journey of the world's birds to the faraway peaks of Mount Qaf--a mythical mountain that wraps around the earth--in search of their king, the mysterious Simorgh. Attar's beguiling anecdotes and humor intermingle the sublime with the mundane, the spiritual with the worldly, and the rel...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges lists Attar's literary works, including the Conference of the Birds, which contains the Simurgh legend.
Jorge Luis Borges cites Attar's 'Conference of the Birds' as an example of a narrative about unity, contrasting it with Stevenson's dualism.
Jorge Luis Borges references the Persian poet Attar and his work 'The Conference of the Birds' to illustrate the principle of identity where the seekers become what they seek.
Jorge Luis Borges discusses Attar as the creator of the Simurgh in the Conference of the Birds, noting his life and works.

book:web_cab95509.description: A foundational work on Buddhism by German Buddhist scholar Georg Grimm, presenting Buddhist doctrine and philosophy.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Grimm's book on Buddhist teachings to explain the process of eliminating the self, noting its excellence.

book:157118.description:
Throughout history philosophers have sought to define, understand, and delineate concepts important to human well-being. One such concept is "knowledge." Many philosophers believed that absolute, certain knowledge, is possible--that the physical world and ideas formulated about it could be given solid foundation unaffected by the varieties of mere opinion.
Sextus Empiricus stands as an example of the "skeptic" school of thought whose members believed that knowledge was either unattainable or, if a genuine p...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Sextus Empiricus's 'Hypotyposes' as an example of using infinite regression to argue against the validity of definitions.

book:2506738.description: Juan Moreira fue publicado por La Patria Argentina en forma de folletin del 28 de noviembre de 1879 al 8 de enero de 1880. Se trata de la obra mas conocida de Eduardo Gutierrez y una de las cumbres del romanticismo literario latinoamericano. Esta novela por entregas, inspirada en una cronica policial que explicaba la muerte de un gaucho, obtuvo un exito enorme e inmediato entre los lectores. Cuatro anos despues, Gutierrez reescribio su obra como "microdrama" para ser representada en el circo. Ha sido llevad...
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges mentions Gutierrez's gaucho novels and Borges's comparison to Cooper.

book:19554254.description: And to be true, and speak my soul, when I survey the occurrences of my life, and call into account the Finger of GOD, I can perceive nothing but an abyss and mass of mercies, either in general to mankind, or in particular to my self. Jorge Luis Borges cites Browne's 'Religio Medici' as a source confirming the metaphor of nature as a divine book.

book:web_b971071d.description: A narrative poem by William Morris retelling the story of Jason and the Argonauts.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges uses this book as a primary example to analyze narrative techniques, specifically focusing on Morris's method of making mythical elements believable.

book:24357337.description:
Wilkie Collins's enthralling story of the cursed diamond stolen from an Indian shrine is the first and probably finest work of detective fiction in the language.
The exquisite Moonstone, a diamond that brings bad luck to whoever has it in their possession, is given to Rachel Verinder for her eighteenth birthday. To the dismay of her family, it is stolen from her that very same night. Sergeant Cuff is brought in to investigate and, with the help of Gabriel Betteredge, the family steward, he becomes aware of....
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Collins' novel as an example of a detective story that verges on psychological fiction.

book:5891.description: Mistaken identities, locked rooms, madness, and romance--these are a few of the ingredients the author (one of the most successful and popular Victorian writers) used to inspire "the 'creepy' effect, as of pounded ice dropped down the back," that, according to one of his friends, was Wilkie Collins's aim in writing The Woman in White. commentaries: Susan Sontag references Collins's novel as an example of a work that explores the tension between female beauty and intelligence, specifically describing the character Marian Halcombe.

book:877693.description: Don Juan Tenorio, el drama romantico por excelencia, es una de las pocas obras que han tenido y siguen teniendo una vida autenticamente popular. Dificil seria encontrar un espanol que no sepa recitar de memoria alguno de sus versos. commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges references Zorrilla's play as another example of the Don Juan literary tradition.

book:web_ebeec15b.description: A classic science fiction fix-up novel by Ray Bradbury, depicting the colonization of Mars by humans fleeing a troubled Earth. It is composed of interconnected short stories.

book:web_43030461.description: A collection of poems by Stefan George, considered a central work of the George Circle and German Symbolist literature.

book:1216209.description:
Heimskringla(Icelandic pronunciation: ['heims,khriNGla]) is the best known of the Old Norse kings' sagas. commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Alvarez's work as a key reference on Argentine Spanish, noting its publication year and place.

book:web_a56a0633.description: A collection of essays on Spanish literature by the Mexican writer and diplomat Alfonso Reyes.
commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges quotes from Reyes's book to support an observation about Quevedo's political works, citing a specific page.

book:web_5325ab73.description: A German-language collection and commentary on the pre-Socratic philosophers, edited and translated by Wilhelm Capelle. The work compiles fragments and testimonia of early Greek philosophers.

commentaries: Jorge Luis Borges cites Toulet's 'Contrerimes', noting its technical perfection and Borges's preference for Toulet over Baudelaire.

book:web_e42de7ea.description: A theological summary by Saint Bonaventure, written around 1257, presenting a concise exposition of Christian doctrine. The work is known for its mystical approach and integration of philosophy with theology.

One of the great masterpieces of Western religious thought, the Zohar represents an attempt to uncover hidden meanings behind the world of appearances. It is the central work in the literature of the Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.
